lessons.title: Feed analysis and the value of feeds
lessons.html:
Reading a feed analysis

At supervisor level you must be able to compare feeds by their nutrient value, not only by price per bag. Laboratories analyse feeds using the proximate (Weende) analysis, and the results appear on feed labels and test reports.

ComponentWhat it tells you
Moisture / dry matter (DM)How much of the feed is water. Always compare feeds on a DM basis.
Crude protein (CP)Estimated from nitrogen content; includes true protein and non-protein nitrogen.
Ether extract (crude fat)Fat and oil, a concentrated energy source.
Crude fibre (or NDF and ADF)Cell-wall material; higher fibre usually means lower digestibility.
AshTotal mineral content.
Nitrogen-free extractStarches and sugars, calculated by difference.

Why dry matter matters

Silage may be about two-thirds water while hay is mostly dry matter. A tonne of silage therefore supplies far fewer nutrients than a tonne of hay. Convert values to DM before comparing feeds or calculating rations.

Energy

Energy is expressed as total digestible nutrients (TDN) or, more precisely, as metabolisable energy (ME) in megajoules per kilogram of DM (MJ/kg DM). Gross energy is lost in dung, urine and rumen gases; ME is what remains for the animal to use for maintenance, growth, milk and work.

Protein for ruminants

  • Rumen-degradable protein (RDP) feeds the rumen microbes. Non-protein nitrogen such as urea can supply part of this.
  • Undegradable (bypass) protein (UDP) passes the rumen and is digested in the small intestine. High-producing dairy cows and fast-growing animals need more bypass protein.

Digestibility

Digestibility is the share of the feed that is not lost in the dung. Young, leafy grass is highly digestible; mature winter veld and straw are poorly digestible, which limits how much the animal can eat.

In South Africa, farm feeds sold commercially must be registered under the Fertilizers, Farm Feeds, Agricultural Remedies and Stock Remedies Act 36 of 1947, and the label must show the guaranteed analysis. Use it.

lessons.title: Nutrient requirements and ration formulation
lessons.html:
What determines requirements?

An animal's nutrient requirement depends on:

  • Maintenance - body mass, activity (walking far on extensive veld raises needs) and climate.
  • Production - rate of growth, milk yield and milk composition, wool growth, work.
  • Reproduction - late pregnancy greatly increases needs; twins increase them further.
  • Age and species - young animals need more protein per kilogram of body mass.

Requirements are published in feeding standards (for example NRC tables) and are applied by nutritionists and feed companies. Dry matter intake limits how much can be supplied: low-quality roughage fills the rumen before needs are met.

Formulating a simple ration: the Pearson square

The Pearson square mixes two feeds to reach a target nutrient level. Example: mix maize (9 percent CP) and oilcake (45 percent CP) to make a 16 percent CP mix.

  1. Write the target (16) in the centre of a square, maize (9) top left and oilcake (45) bottom left.
  2. Subtract across the diagonals, ignoring minus signs: 45 minus 16 gives 29 parts maize; 16 minus 9 gives 7 parts oilcake.
  3. Total parts = 36. Maize = 29 divided by 36 = about 80.6 percent; oilcake = 7 divided by 36 = about 19.4 percent.
  4. Check: 0.806 x 9 plus 0.194 x 45 gives about 16 percent CP.

The target must lie between the two feed values. The square balances only one nutrient, so energy, minerals and fibre must still be checked. For complex rations, farms use a nutritionist and least-cost formulation software.

Cost per nutrient

Compare feeds by cost per kilogram of protein or per MJ of energy, not per bag. A cheaper feed that is wet or low in protein may cost more per unit of nutrient delivered.

Supplementation strategy

  • Winter dry veld: protein (often with NPN) to improve fibre digestion and intake.
  • Summer veld: phosphorus and salt.
  • Production animals: energy and bypass protein.

lessons.title: Nutritional disorders and feed management
lessons.html:
Common nutritional disorders

DisorderCausePrevention
Rumen acidosisSudden intake of large amounts of grain or starchAdapt gradually; enough roughage; control access
BloatFoam or gas trapped in the rumen, often on lush legumesFill animals with roughage before grazing lucerne; anti-bloat products per label
Urea (NPN) poisoningToo much urea, poorly mixed licks, hungry animalsMix correctly; introduce slowly; protect licks from rain
Phosphorus deficiencyLow-P veld; leads to pica and botulism riskPhosphate licks; vaccinate against botulism as the vet advises
Milk feverLow blood calcium around calvingCorrect dry-cow minerals per nutritionist
Grass tetanyLow blood magnesium on lush pastureMagnesium supplementation on high-risk pastures
Copper poisoning in sheepSheep fed rations or licks meant for cattle or pigsUse only sheep-specific products for sheep

Antinutritional factors and toxins

  • Raw soya beans contain trypsin inhibitors; they must be heat-treated for monogastrics.
  • Mouldy grain and hay may contain mycotoxins that reduce growth, fertility and immunity.
  • Some plants accumulate nitrate or prussic acid, for example stressed sorghum. Get advice before grazing drought-stressed or frosted crops.
  • Poisonous plants such as tulp, gifblaar and slangkop cause serious stock losses; hungry animals and newly introduced stock are most at risk.

Feed management and quality control

  • Inspect deliveries: check labels, registration numbers, smell, colour and moisture.
  • Store feed off the floor, dry, ventilated and protected from rodents and birds.
  • Use first-in, first-out stock rotation.
  • Keep stock remedies, fertilisers and pesticides well away from feed.
  • Take samples for analysis when buying large lots of hay or silage.
  • Monitor results through body condition scoring, weighing, milk records and dung consistency, and adjust rations.

Key points

  • Compare feeds on a dry matter basis using the label analysis.
  • Energy is measured as TDN or ME; ruminant protein is split into RDP and bypass protein.
  • The Pearson square balances one nutrient between two feeds.
  • Compare feeds by cost per unit of nutrient.
  • Prevent acidosis, bloat and urea poisoning through gradual change and correct mixing.
  • Never give sheep products meant for cattle or pigs, because of copper.
